articles.title: A new movie asks whether Chris Hansen is the predator. He's sure of his answer.
articles.summary: "Primetime" shows him as overzealous. The cops on a recent sting in Louisiana are happy to have his help.
articles.body:
LIVINGSTON PARISH, La. — Chris Hansen hops into a gray SUV to head to the sting house. He doesn't have a driver. He doesn't have a news network expense account, not anymore. But he has that face, that voice, and so it's hard to go anywhere without getting noticed.

"Can I bug you for a picture?" a woman asks when he stops at a Starbucks to buy coffee for his crew.

Heather Smith-David watched "To Catch a Predator" religiously on "Dateline NBC." The segment, which ran from 2004 to 2007, took on added significance for her a few years ago, when she says a man attacked her teenage son and tried to sexually assault him.

Your weekly guide to culture, entertainment, and what everyone is talking about. Sign up for free

"I'm so sorry to hear that," Hansen calmly tells her, in a tone somewhere between Edward R. Murrow and Superman. "That's why we do it."

During these fan interactions, Hansen will first ask the admirer to hold off on posting a photo for a few days. He doesn't want to tip off the bad guys that he's in town. He also usually plugs the successor to the long-defunct "Predator," his streaming series called "Takedown with Chris Hansen." But there's no need with Smith-David. She's already subscribing to TruBlu, Hansen's online crime-themed network.

To some, Hansen is an overzealous TV hack, a predator of predators, thrilled to ruin the lives of people who never so much as touched a child. To Smith-David, Hansen is a crusader against evil. He's confronting the men who walk into a sting house hoping to have sex with minors — and getting them locked up.

This month, Hansen's subscription base should get a boost. A24's "Primetime," in which he's portrayed by Robert Pattinson, opened in theaters on Friday. Hansen wasn't consulted by the filmmakers, and his plan to see an advance screening fizzled when he wouldn't sign the studio's nondisclosure agreement. He figured he'd show up at the box office and buy a ticket; he'd agree to have The Washington Post come along. As for A24's publicity campaign, Hansen figured he'd co-opt it for his own means.

In the run-up to the release, he went on Fox News with Jesse Watters to blast A24, told the Hollywood Reporter that the film is an "insult" and continued the scolding on his podcast, "Predators I've Caught." Shawn Rech, his business partner, urged Hansen to sue, but for now, they've settled on an alternative. TruBlu bought ad space so that screenings of "Primetime" will be introduced by a commercial featuring Hansen.

"It's evil and unethical, what they're doing," Rech says. "But I told Chris there's an opportunity here. We need to come out of this with people knowing you're still doing this."

The sting house set up for this episode of his online show is half an hour east of Baton Rouge in a town called Walker. Hansen drives until he's in a neighborhood with large, scrubby yards and single-level homes. Inside the house, he's greeted by Capt. Calvin Bowden of the Livingston Parish Sheriff's Office, whose detectives and decoys are already stuffed in a back room on laptops and iPads talking dirty with a steady stream of online suspects. Bowden borrowed the place, which is for sale, from a real estate broker. It looks lived in, with corny, lettered sayings on the walls ("This is us") and appliances and furniture still in place. Hansen's crew has wired the property with hidden cameras, which two cameramen monitor on a screen in the primary bedroom.

The plan is that when a suspect approaches, the decoy will lure him — and it's always a him, no woman has been caught in 22 years — into the living room, and then Hansen, huddled in a kitchen pantry with his camera guys, will emerge and deliver his patented command to "take a seat."

Over the 20 episodes on "Dateline" and intermittently during the two decades since, he's been part of dozens of busts with men thinking they're about to meet a minor for sex. Hansen calmly picks the suspects apart with questions about their intentions and, when they inevitably deny that they planned to do anything sexual, confronts them with their own words, reading back the transcripts of the chats. Over time, Hansen says, he's been involved in more than 500 arrests, watching as religious leaders ( a rabbi , a Sunday school teacher), lawyers, real estate brokers and military veterans are cuffed and hauled away.

"We could end up with one guy today, we could end up with six or seven people today," Hansen says just after arriving at the house. "We don't choose these guys, they choose us."

That could also describe how Hansen morphed from a rising network correspondent metabolically drawn to the big story — Oklahoma City, Columbine, 9/11 — into someone forever associated with the pedophile beat. He never planned on this. Hansen, 67, grew up during the golden age of TV news, admiring the way "60 Minutes" star Mike Wallace confronted wrongdoers. He started reporting while still at Michigan State University, worked in local news for a decade and landed at NBC in 1993.

At the network, Hansen earned a slew of Emmys, but it was "To Catch a Predator" that made him famous. The Pattinson film takes its name from NBC's decision to run "Dateline" in prime time, where it sometimes competed with ABC's science-fiction drama "Lost." By then, Hansen was appearing with Oprah Winfrey, Conan O'Brien and Jon Stewart as well as dropping into "The Simpsons" and "South Park." One night in 2009, he sat in the audience at "Saturday Night Live" as Bill Hader delivered a perfectly modulated impression in a sketch called "Late Night with Chris Hansen," which found the host springing on his celebrity guests and ending their appearances with a police tackle.

The real-life Hansen was only a little less theatrical. As the show developed, it fed on the absurdity, all the better as his voice rose to ask, "What were you thinking ?" In one episode, a man told a decoy he wanted to watch her commit a sex act with a cat and Cool Whip and stripped off his clothes as he entered the house. "Do you want to explain yourself?" Hansen mugged as he confronted him.

The whole thing was masterful as sensationalistic TV, cringe-inducing, hilarious and horrifying, which is why chuckling YouTubers still make a habit of splicing commentary between reposted segments. What these encounters weren't, says Kelly McBride, the chief ethicist at the Poynter Institute and NPR's public editor, was journalism.

"Advocacy pretending to be journalism," says McBride, who has watched Hansen's work for decades. "And there's a level of shame and humiliation as entertainment that is core to what he's doing."

One of McBride's main complaints is Hansen's cozy relationship with law enforcement. Journalists are taught that while it's good to have a communicative relationship with police, they are not themselves a policing force. There needs to be a firm line between the reporting and the investigation and arrest. The criticism that Hansen blurs that line has hounded him since a disastrous 2006 incident in Murphy, Texas, that led to a suspect, Rockland County assistant district attorney Bill Conradt, killing himself as police moved in on him.

"Primetime" is adapted, in part, from a 2009 Esquire story detailing the incident, "Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die."

"A hatchet job," Hansen says of Luke Dittrich's story. (Dittrich, as well as Pattinson and director Lance Oppenheim, declined interview requests through A24.)

Oppenheim also consulted David Osit, who made a 2025 documentary, "Predators," that Hansen felt left out key information about the Conradt case, specifically the child sexual abuse material found on his computer.

That operation led to the arrests of more than 20 men at the sting house. But Conradt, who had chatted with one of the decoys, never headed over. So instead, the police and "Dateline's" team went to him on a Sunday afternoon. They gathered outside as a SWAT team entered to find Conradt standing in a hallway, holding a gun. "He told them he wasn't going to hurt them and shot himself in the head," Lt. Adana Barber told Hansen on camera.

In the Esquire story and an investigation on ABC's "20/20," Hansen is portrayed as so thirsty to capture Conradt that he and Perverted Justice, which styled itself as a computer watchdog group, worked in sync with police to confront him. At one point, video shows Hansen reading Conradt's phone number to a police officer so he can make contact within the house. Conradt's sister, Patricia, sued NBC for $105 million. The case was settled; she told The Post that she could not comment.

In the end, none of the others arrested in Murphy were prosecuted, as prosecutors dismissed the investigations conducted by Perverted Justice.

McBride points out that studies show the majority of cases are committed by adults the victims know, not strangers showing up to a sting house.

"I am not going to deny that it happens, and I'm not going to deny that it's horrible," she says. "But focusing on that does not help us reduce the incidence of child sexual abuse."

The whole thing started with a call from a friend in Detroit. Kevin Dietz, an investigative reporter for an NBC affiliate TV station, had partnered with Perverted Justice, which was using volunteer decoys as part of its advocacy-slash-vigilante operation to engage men on the internet looking to have sex with minors. WDIV (Channel 4) ran the piece during sweeps early in 2004 and scored big ratings. "There's something here, Chris," Dietz remembers telling Hansen. "And he knew there was something there. He just didn't know what it was and if [the network] would go for it, quite frankly."

But Hansen doesn't remember much resistance.

He was 44, a decade into a respected career at NBC. By the time he pitched his bosses on confronting possible predators on camera, hidden-camera reality shows were thriving. "Survivor" and "Big Brother" documented the sociological drama of groupthink, HBO's "Taxicab Confessions" talked dirty, and Ashton Kutcher's "Punk'd" let the "That '70s Show" star prank his fellow celebrities. TV newsmagazines were also changing from the "60 Minutes" model. Neal Shapiro, installed to oversee "Dateline," moved the show from one night a week to five in 1998. He was impressed by Hansen's doggedness but also his gift for the two-camera interview.

"That's what makes newsmagazines different from other kinds of journalism," Shapiro says. "This is a skill all of its own. You can't stumble around, you have to be quick, you have to be fast on your feet and on the investigative front, really listening and drawing people out. He was very good at that."

Still, doing the undercover pedophile stings was a departure for "Dateline." Hansen remembers his boss, David Corvo, questioning how the network could possibly promote the segment.

"How about, there's a guy standing in your back porch with his d--- in his hand, he wants to stick it in your daughter, and tonight we're going to show you how to prevent that from happening," Hansen says he told Corvo.

The first episode was called "Dangerous Web," opening with anchor Stone Phillips framing the segment as a wake-up call to parents about the dangers of web surfing and internet chatrooms. "Dateline" rented a white house on a main street in Bethpage, New York, and installed a pair of Perverted Justice decoys and hidden cameras. The men caught included a New York City firefighter, who was fired from the department and pleaded guilty for sending obscene photos to a minor.

But the firefighter was an exception. Most of the people caught in the first sting were not prosecuted, largely because the police weren't involved yet.

That was also the case in the second episode, filmed outside Washington, D.C., which introduced a slightly softer version of what would become Hansen's catchphrase, as he walked into the room and confronted the visitor with, "Why don't you have a seat?" The segment also featured a man who took off his clothes before entering the house. Hansen handed him a towel and later delivered one of his signature lines: "What would have happened if I wasn't here?"

By that point, other networks were trying to lure Perverted Justice away from NBC, and Xavier Von Erck, the organization's founder, remembers being flown first class to Los Angeles for a steakhouse dinner with NBC chief executive Jeff Zucker. In "Primetime," the former executive — playing himself — tells Hansen he doesn't like the show. In real life, Von Erck remembers "not a single word other than, 'We love you guys, this is so important, and we want you to sign a deal.'" (Zucker did not respond to an interview request.)

In fact, NBC invested plenty in Hansen's franchise, which was becoming a ratings bonanza. Under Zucker, the network began paying Perverted Justice $100,000 for each sting. It also approved partnering with police, which led to the arrests and the dramatic finales for the stings — and ever more viewers. After Hansen finished his interview, the suspect would invariably ask whether he was free to go. Hansen would nod or signal toward the door with his hand. And outside the police would be waiting, often to tackle the man and cuff him. The televised setup was still entrapment, defense attorneys and critics would argue, but with law enforcement now making arrests, the conviction rate improved.

There would be 12 undercover operations in total before "To Catch a Predator" was canceled in 2008 after the negative scrutiny and legal pressure that followed the Conradt case. Hansen says that the show had "just run its course." Von Erck thinks there was another reason. As popular as "To Catch a Predator" was with viewers, advertisers were spooked.

"We used to have guys bring a product called Mike's Hard Lemonade to the houses because they were advertising all the time back then," Von Erck says. "Usually, product placement is a wonderful thing for most TV shows. Mike's Hard Lemonade sent a cease and desist to 'Dateline' asking them never to mention their product again."

When Hollywood wants to really deliver the nuance and the authenticity, the flaws and the understanding, of a living character, it tends to reach out at least minimally to the party being portrayed.

To research her role in "Selena," Jennifer Lopez stayed with the singer's sister in Corpus Christi, Texas, and even slept in the late pop star's bed. Christian Bale spent months in Lowell, Massachusetts, walking the streets with Dicky Eklund as he prepared to play him in "The Fighter." Margot Robbie flew out to meet figure skater Tonya Harding before filming started on "I, Tonya" and invited her to walk the red carpet for the film's premiere.

Pattinson and Hansen have never met and never exchanged so much as a text message.

It was only in May, a day before A24 released "Primetime's" first teaser, that the studio reached out to Hansen. Sure, he had heard rumblings. Kevin Balfe, one of the founders of Red Seat Ventures, which represents Hansen, had even heard from director Oppenheim, who told him that the film was a "love letter" to Hansen.

The man at the center of the film had his doubts. He wanted to see a script. He was eager to watch an early version. Then he learned Osit, who had made the 2025 documentary, "Predators," which Hansen considered unflattering, was pals with Oppenheim and had seen a cut — without signing an NDA.

In August, A24 contacted Hansen, inviting him to see the film at its offices in New York City. But the studio wanted him to sign the NDA before "Primetime" screened. He showed up that day and, as he'd intended, rejected its request. That set his real plan into motion. After a lot of haggling and no compromise from either side, he headed to Fox News to blast the filmmakers.

At lunch in New York next to Red Seat's offices, Hansen talks about what he considers A24's disingenuous approach.

"The press woman calls, 'I talked to Robert, he's in London, and I talked to Lance, and they really want you to be happy,'" Hansen recounts. "'And Robert's going to come on your podcast if you want to go to London, where he's shooting the next Batman movie.' I mean, they talked to me like I'm a little kid. You know, 'Oh, God, my name's going to be in a movie.' I've been in this business for 45 years. The least they can f---ing do is if you're going to take somebody's name, image and likeness, have the courtesy of showing them the film without making them sign an NDA. They didn't sign any permission to use my name, image and likeness."

Was he "furious" as the New York Post reported soon after in a headline?

"I'm busy being the real Chris Hansen every day," he says. "I don't have time."

When you see the film, it'll be clear why Oppenheim and Pattinson didn't want Hansen hanging around the set or writer's room.

"Primetime" is a dynamic, visual feast, with a stellar performance from the actor. The director soaks the atmosphere in the video age, the shots fuzzy and often marked with time codes as if you're watching through a camcorder's viewfinder. But the script plays loose with the facts. Von Erck is a central character, present at all shoots and driving the decision-making as much as Hansen's NBC producer. In reality, Von Erck says he wasn't on a single sting.

Equally unflattering is the portrayal of Hansen's producer. The real producer, Lynn Keller, is turned into a character named Andie Bender, a careerist whose main response to a man killing himself is to offer, "I think I can use this." (Keller, still at NBC, did not respond to an interview request.)

And the film is certainly no "love letter." Hansen is driven by insecurity as he interacts with snooty anchor Phillips and Zucker. He's also a mess at home. He wakes his arguably too-young-to-watch-this boys so they can screen "Predator." He lies to his wife and has an affair that lands him in the National Enquirer. As "Primetime" presents it, Hansen's mission is simply to rule his time slot, a slick, self-absorbed philanderer trying to become a star. In the Conradt case, he's not simply a bystander. He's the protagonist.

So is Hansen driven by ego? Is he too close to the police? Is this high theater or advocacy? And is he helping parents or merely helping himself?

Osit believes that Hansen and the slew of copycats who emerged after him weren't interested in solving the root cause of child sexual abuse.

"The way that the show operates is that we can see that these people are irredeemably sick beyond help," he says. "And then as a result, we don't really care what happens to them as a society."

But Hansen says he's not a counselor or a therapist. He is a "working reporter" doing "enterprise journalism." He made the decision long ago to work with police for what he calls "a greater good — to be socially responsible and ensure these guys face justice."

There are times, he says, a suspect's sad life story can elicit sympathy.

"But at the same time that doesn't excuse somebody trying to exploit a vulnerable child," Hansen says. "He knows better. He's an adult. There's a hundred places he could be."

After NBC canceled the show in 2008, Hansen remained at "Dateline." But in 2011, the National Enquirer's hidden cameras caught him in an affair with a younger TV reporter in Florida. In 2013, that woman, no longer with Hansen, told her story to Radar Online and included a photograph of the two kissing. Hansen was laid off from NBC soon after, and he and his first wife, Mary Joan, separated and eventually divorced. For a few years, Hansen bounced around, doing a show on Discovery, a series, "Hansen vs. Predator," for Crime Watch Daily, and in 2019, launching a YouTube channel. He also hit some bumps that landed him in the tabloids again for bouncing checks and defaulting on his rent.

This is the one chapter that Hansen tightens up over. His explanation is limited.

"It's a time when a lot of things were happening, a divorce, a lot of transition and it's not even worth analyzing," he says. "You fix it, you take care of it and you move on."

On his own and free of network oversight, Hansen doesn't pretend there's much of a wall between him and the police. In Louisiana, he's greeted in the sting house as both a peer and folk hero. Other detectives bring items to Hansen — custom-made medallions, handcuffs, a mug — that he can autograph during downtime. They need each other. Without the police, he can't gather more sting content. Without Hansen, they can't get much buzz beyond articles in local newspapers.

What's also interesting about the sting is how little Hansen is involved. He spends most of the time in the kitchen or living room, scrolling on his phone, talking to colleagues about upcoming recordings or warming up yet another cup of coffee in the microwave. The action takes place in a cramped back room, where half a dozen detectives and decoys sit under mounted deer heads as they bounce from laptops to iPads. The engagements usually start by posting a basic photo of the decoy on a social media site. Then the detectives juggle chats with anywhere from 15 to 20 men at a time. The male officers wear tight blue golf shirts with their names sewn in. The female decoys wear sweats and tank tops. At any moment, they may have to repair to one of the two bedrooms and go into decoy mode, chatting with a suspect.

There are rules on this day, meant to make prosecutions fairer and smoother. The law enforcement decoys engage only with men 21 and older. They have to depict themselves as being younger than 17, which is the age of consent for sexual activity in Louisiana. They aren't allowed to entrap the men by suggesting sex acts first or inviting them over. The men have to suggest the visit.

The sting nets two men on this day. One arrives wearing an ankle bracelet from another case. He insists, when Hansen confronts him, that he merely wanted to come and watch the budget-core horror flick "Obsession" with the 15-year-old because he has no WiFi at home.

The other person caught in the sting is a 21-year-old diesel mechanic. He gives fair warning as he drives up; his bright yellow pickup truck roars as he makes his way down the driveway. He walks in with a loaded gun tucked into his pants. Because of that, Hansen has to abandon the standard approach. Instead, Capt. Bowden of the Livingston Parish Sheriff's Office approaches first, disarming the suspect with ease. Now at the couch, Hansen approaches him and begins to run through his questions. The man has only an eighth-grade education. He's upset because he knows he's going to get fired from his job.

Hansen starts by asking him why he came here.

"Originally, I came over here just to meet somebody new," he says. "If we were friends, I didn't find anything wrong."

"But you talk about … touching her butt and taking showers together," Hansen says. "Do you see how this looks?"

"I don't know," he answers. "I can't afford to leave this job."

"You should have thought about that before you came over here to have sex with a child," Hansen says. "You're a man. You should be out doing man things. Taking out women of appropriate age. Working on diesel. Drilling for oil. Stuff men do. Not raping a child."

When he's done, Bowden steps in, on camera. He's got a few lines before the scene wraps.

"What we don't like is people coming to this parish to exploit our children, and Sheriff Jason Ard, he don't put up with that," Bowden says. "And you know what, he's here today."

Ard, waiting in the wings for his cameo, steps forward.

"We're going to bring you down to my hotel motel," Ard says, "and you can do all the rub-a-dub-dubs you want in that jail. We got plenty of showers for you."

"Holy s---," a woman shouts as she exits the 7:10 p.m. showing of "Primetime" in Times Square. "It's Chris Hansen."

This wasn't quite the red carpet premiere at the Venice Film Festival. At the Regal, the escalator is busted, the air conditioning seems to be on the fritz and Hansen has to throw down $24.68 for a seat in Row G.

His wife, Gabrielle Hansen, has come along, but this isn't a date night. A small crew tails him to capture his reaction to the movie, which he is seeing for the first time.

When the lights come on, he acknowledges he didn't know what to make of Oppenheim's film. There were occasional moments of truth, but most of the script was fiction.

Outside the Regal, a crowd assembles. They watch as the real Chris Hansen starts conducting interviews.

"I'm interested in seeing how he feels about seeing that," says one man, Eric Ingram. "He did not look good in that film. I found it really disturbing watching it."

Anyone expecting an emotional response from Hansen wasn't going to get it.

"It was so dark and so twisted, it was hard for me to take seriously," he says.

For 45 minutes, he does what he came here to do: gather content. Video would be posted all weekend by his social team. Interviews were cut for his podcast. Then there was another Fox News appearance with Watters.

After her husband wraps up a last selfie, Gabrielle Hansen complains that the film had been insulting. Chris Hansen seems unconcerned. "I've been in this business a long time, and I knew what this was going to be," he says.

As the couple begins walking, heading to get a bite to eat, he shrugs.

Aaron Schaffer contributed to this report.

articles.title: Dakota Johnson has snarky 3-word reply for people speculating about her love life amid rumored MGK romance
articles.summary: “People are gonna believe what they wanna believe,” she said on “The Run-Through” podcast.
articles.body:
Dakota Johnson is addressing the speculation surrounding her dating life.

During a visit to The Run-Through podcast, Johnson explained why she doesn't bother to shut down false rumors.

"People are gonna believe what they wanna believe," she insisted.

The speculation may rage on, but Dakota Johnson is keeping her dating life to herself.

The Verity actress is well aware of the gossip surrounding her personal life but insists that there's no point in clearing up false rumors since new whispers will always take their place.

"Even if I go to dinner with my manager or my lawyer, it's like, 'Seen with mystery man,'" Johnson pointed out during a Sept. 25 episode of Vogue 's The Run-Through podcast. "I also don't care."

Asked if she ever feels the need to step in and set the record straight, Johnson replied, "I think it's just futile. People are gonna believe what they wanna believe, and I don't have the energy to fight for that."

Johnson added that she "would much rather" put her focus elsewhere.

"Every day, there's something on the internet that's ridiculous and true or not true, and I don't care," she said.

Currently, the raging speculation surrounds Johnson's rumored romance with rapper Machine Gun Kelly , with sources claiming that the duo noticed a spark while attending Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce 's summer wedding at Madison Square Garden.

Ultimately, Johnson didn't address any specific rumors on the podcast. But she did share a snarky three-word message for those pondering her romantic entanglements: "Get a life," she said.

As for her relationship to social media, as someone frequently in the spotlight, the Materialists star said she does her best to avoid scrolling.

"Maybe when I was in my younger 20s, I had a moment of being on social media just for fun and laughs," she said. "'Cause I love a clever thing. But I just don't f--k with it."

Johnson added that while there is a level of engagement that she can't avoid, as she sometimes needs social media"for work," she otherwise steers clear.

"I feel really uncomfortable with the constant documenting of people's lives," she said.

Neither Johnson nor MGK, whose real name is Colson Baker, have addressed the budding relationship, but earlier this month a source told PEOPLE that the pair "hit it off" at the Swift-Kelce wedding and have been spending time together "under the radar for months." The duo have since been photographed out and about in New York City.

Johnson added some fuel to the fire during a recent Vogue interview, in which she was asked about her history of dating musicians.

"They like me," Johnson said, a reference to her romantic links with Coldplay frontman Chris Martin and indie singer Role Model. "I don't know what to say. And I like them."

The interviewer replied, "What's not to like?"

Johnson then quipped, "A lot! A lot. Tricky motherf---ers."

Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter .

Elsewhere in the conversation, the actress explained her desire for privacy, sharing that she prefers to keep her daily life on the down-low.

"I am obsessed with people not knowing where I am or what I'm doing," she said. "I'm far too porous and sensitive and present. I don't — I can't deal."

articles.title: Meet Barron Trump's college girlfriend — all we know about 6ft 9 student's life on campus
articles.summary: Donald Trump's son, Barron, reportedly has a college girlfriend and here's what we know about his love life
articles.body:
Barron Trump, son of US President Donald Trump, has reportedly been quietly dating a girlfriend he met at New York University for over a year now.

Barron transferred to NYU's DC campus in September 2026 to be closer to his parents, but it is unclear if he is still dating the woman.

Despite being described as shy and reserved, Barron Trump has shown a bold and entertaining personality, impressing guests at a dinner event in 2025.

Barron Trump , the 20-year-old son of the President of the United States, was perhaps the most eligible bachelor at New York University - until now!

The college student has reportedly found love with a girlfriend whom he met at college, with multiple outlets reporting that the pair have been quietly dating for over a year now

While not much is known about the woman in question, Barron spent the first year of college studying at New York University's Stern School of Business which is based on the Greenwich Village campus. He didn't live on campus but instead commuted from Trump Tower in Manhattan

In October 2024, Donald appeared on the PBD podcast and was quizzed over his son's love life, admitting at the time he was not sure Barron was "there yet," adding: " I don't think he's had a girlfriend yet."

However, in September 2026 it was confirmed that Barron had transferred to the school's DC campus for at least one semester to be closer to his mother and father. It is unclear if he is still dating the woman.

Interest in Barron's dating life began when a TikToker named Maddie said Barron was her "first BF" when they attended high school together.

She posted a video that featured clips of herself and Barron together, and claimed they'd broken up when Barron moved to attend St. Andrews Potomac in Virginia.

Barron has been linked to other 'girlfriends' in the past, including Sarah Claire and a model Klara Jones, who is two years older than him.

While Barron prefers to stay out of the spotlight, and has long been touted as "shy and reserved," it appears that is no longer the case. In 2025, Barron spoke about his father during a dinner at Mar-a-Lago and guests were blown away by his boldness.

American entrepreneur, Patrick Bet-David, attended the event, along with Tom Ellsworth and actor and comedian Vincent Oshana.

They dissected what they witnessed on an episode of Patrick's PBD podcast when they recalled watching "Barron run dinner with stories, entertainment, everything," for 90 minutes straight.

"I've never seen Tom laugh this hard for an hour and a half," Patrick said.

Vincent was left in awe of the teen's ability to keep the audience's attention and said: "He's 18. He's witty, smart, hilarious. He was smart on politics. He's like 'You know, everybody's always going to fight. There's left. There's right.'"

Vincent said Barron has a "good head on his shoulders." He was also branded: "Sharp, funny, sarcastic and tough."

Barron's first year in New York City was not the usual first year for a college students. Reports claimed that he was unable to make friends or enjoy a normal life as he was shadowed 24/7 by security and entered and exited the building through garages and secret doors.

Kaya Walker, the then-president of the NYU College Republicans, said in a 2025 interview that Barron was an "oddity" who "goes to class, he goes home." Other students claimed that they had invited him to pick-up basketball games and although he was interested he never confirmed plans.

articles.title: Idosos de Óbidos visitam Alter do Chão em excursão de lazer | G1
articles.standfirst: Grupo saiu de Óbidos na noite de sexta-feira (25) e passou o fim de semana na vila. Para parte dos participantes, foi a primeira vez no destino turístico.
articles.summary: O grupo de idosos de Óbidos aproveitou o fim de semana com hidroginástica e visitas turísticas em Alter do Chão, marcando a primeira viagem de muitos ao local.
articles.body:
Idosos de Óbidos aproveitaram o passeio em Alter do Chão, em Santarém, durante o fim de semana — Foto: Odirlei Santos/ ASCOM-PMO

Uma viagem de barco levou 178 idosos de Óbidos, no oeste do Pará, até a vila de Alter do Chão, em Santarém, para um fim de semana de lazer, atividades físicas e convivência. O grupo saiu de Óbidos na noite de sexta-feira (25) e chegou ao destino no sábado (26).

A viagem foi organizada para reunir idosos que participam de atividades sociais e de saúde em diferentes comunidades de Óbidos, incluindo moradores da área urbana e da zona rural. Para muitos deles, o passeio representou a oportunidade de conhecer um dos destinos turísticos mais conhecidos do oeste do Pará.

Alter do Chão fica a cerca de 40 km do centro de Santarém e é conhecida pelas praias de água doce, especialmente durante o período de vazante dos rios, quando aparecem as faixas de areia às margens do Tapajós.

Ilha do Amor foi um dos locais visitados pelos 178 idosos durante a viagem — Foto: Odirlei Santos/ ASCOM-PMO

Depois da chegada, o grupo participou de uma programação que misturou atividades físicas, visitas e momentos de convivência com moradores da vila.

Uma das primeiras atividades foi uma aula de hidroginástica realizada na praia. A prática foi acompanhada por momentos de descanso e confraternização entre os participantes.

Os idosos também visitaram o Terminal Turístico de Alter do Chão e o barracão do Boto Tucuxi, uma das agremiações tradicionais que participam do Festival do Sairé.

Viagem também incluiu visita ao barracão do Boto Tucuxi, uma das agremiações tradicionais do Sairé — Foto: Odirlei Santos/ ASCOM/PMO

A programação ainda contou com um encontro entre os idosos de Óbidos e participantes de atividades voltadas à terceira idade em Alter do Chão. O momento serviu para troca de experiências e convivência entre pessoas de municípios diferentes.

Durante o trajeto de barco entre Óbidos e Santarém, os participantes também tiveram música ao vivo e momentos de confraternização.

A aposentada Maria de Lourdes Araújo já havia participado de uma viagem anterior do grupo, quando o destino foi Parintins, no Amazonas. Desta vez, ela aproveitou o passeio em Alter do Chão ao lado dos colegas.

“Eu comecei indo para Parintins, gostei muito, foi maravilhoso, e agora esse aqui, estou adorando estar com meus colegas aqui. É um prazer para todos nós. Estou muito feliz, felicíssima”, contou.

Para o vigia Antônio Vieira, a experiência foi diferente. Ele entrou recentemente no grupo e participou pela primeira vez de uma excursão. Acompanhado da esposa, aproveitou o passeio para conhecer o destino e passar um tempo fora da rotina.

“É a primeira vez que estou participando do passeio e está sendo muito legal para a gente se divertir um pouco, sair de casa, passear e interagir com os colegas”, disse.

A viagem para Alter do Chão foi a terceira excursão realizada com o grupo de idosos de Óbidos. Antes, os participantes já haviam viajado para Terra Santa, no oeste do Pará, e Parintins, no Amazonas.

Além das atividades de lazer, os encontros proporcionam momentos de convivência entre os participantes, muitos deles moradores de comunidades diferentes de Óbidos.

A programação em Alter do Chão terminou na Ilha do Amor, um dos pontos turísticos mais conhecidos da vila.

Para os participantes, o passeio ficou marcado não apenas pelas praias e pelos pontos turísticos visitados, mas também pela oportunidade de viajar juntos, conhecer novos lugares e passar alguns dias fora da rotina.

A ação foi promovida pelo Governo Municipal de Óbidos, por meio de uma ação conjunta entre as secretarias de Desenvolvimento Social e de Saúde, promoveu mais uma edição da excursão de integração e lazer destinada a 178 idosos assistidos pelos programas sociais e pelos grupões de saúde das zonas urbana e rural do município.

articles.title: Roberta Miranda chega aos 70 anos, 40 deles como majestade que abriu alas na dinastia feminina do universo sertanejo | G1
articles.body:
Nascida em 28 de setembro de 1956, a cantora e compositora Roberta Miranda faz 70 anos hoje, segunda-feira — Foto: Reprodução / Instagram Roberta Miranda

♬ Roberta Miranda faz 70 anos hoje, segunda-feira, 28 de setembro. A data merece ser festejada como efeméride da música brasileira diante da importância da cantora e compositora paraibana no universo sertanejo.

Nascida Maria Albuquerque Miranda em João Pessoa (PB), em 28 de setembro de 1956, a artista adotou o nome artístico de Roberta Miranda ao iniciar a carreira fonográfica em 1986 com retumbante sucesso. Sim, dos 70 anos de vida da artista, 40 foram vividos no palco – outra efeméride, esta celebrada em cena pela cantora na turnê “A majestade”, recém-estreada em 19 de setembro, no Rio de Janeiro (RJ).

Sim, Roberta Miranda foi a primeira rainha na dinastia da música sertaneja, desbravando em carreira solo um território historicamente masculino e dominado por duplas formadas por homens. Roberta fez história no universo sertanejo porque extrapolou a função de cantora reservada até então às poucas intérpretes que desafiavam a hegemonia masculina.

Antes de conseguir lançar o primeiro disco, Roberta Miranda foi revelada como compositora em 1985, ano em que a canção “A majestade o sabiá” foi apresentada ao Brasil em álbum do cantor Jair Rodrigues (1939 – 2014), em gravação feita com participação da dupla Chitãozinho & Xororó. E foi como compositora que ela se impôs no mercado sertanejo, lançando álbuns que bateram venderam milhares de cópias entre 1986 e 1992, período áureo da discografia da artista.

A rigor, a primeira música de Roberta Miranda a ganhar registro fonográfico foi “Mãe guerreira”, lançada na voz do cantor Ruy Maurity (1949 – 2022) em 1984. Mas foi mesmo “A majestade o sabiá” a música que abriu as portas da indústria fonográfica para Roberta Miranda.

Em 1986, a artista debutou como cantora com “Roberta Miranda”, álbum blockbuster de repertório autoral que destacou as músicas “São tantas coisas” e “Meu dengo”, esta um baião de sensual pegada forrozeira que evidenciou a origem paraibana da artista.

Em 1987, o segundo álbum – também intitulado “Roberta Miranda”, mas popularmente conhecido como “Volume 2”, como andava a tradição fonográfica sertaneja da época – vendeu ainda mais do que o primeiro, no embalo do sucesso de músicas como “Vá com Deus”.

É fato que a obra autoral de Roberta Miranda não deu voz ativa às mulheres, como Marília Mendonça (1995 – 2021), futura rainha sertaneja, faria nos anos 2010, abrindo novas alas femininas no gênero.

A música de Roberta Miranda não explicitou o gênero feminino nas letras de canções como “Sol da minha vida” (1992). Tanto que um dos maiores sucessos do cancioneiro da compositora, “De igual para igual”, música composta em parceria com Matogrosso, foi lançada na voz do cantor José Augusto em 1987.

Nem por isso Roberta Miranda merece menos loas. Até porque a música da compositora sempre teve uma sensibilidade feminina captada pelo público, que avalizou de imediato a música feita por Roberta Miranda de um jeito particular.

E, cabe ressaltar, Roberta continua em plena atividade nos palcos e nos estúdios, sem nunca ter parado no tempo. Já adaptada ao modus operandi digital do mercado fonográfico, a cantora volta e meia lança single com música inédita. O último single solo, “Os meus 15 anos”, foi lançado em 31 de julho.

Roberta também soube se reinventar nas redes sociais, se posicionando geralmente sem filtro, como no post recente em que criticou o fato de o cantor Rick (1966 – 2026) ter ganhado mais de um milhão de seguidores após a morte em acidente de helicóptero.

Enfim, Roberta Miranda chega firme e forte aos 70 anos, ciente de que já tem um bom lugar todinho dela na história da música sertaneja.

articles.title: Campos do Jordão terá árvore de Natal de 20 metros e 16 km de luzes | G1
articles.standfirst: Programação começa no dia 30 de outubro, com a chegada do Papai Noel.
articles.summary: Programação começa no dia 30 de outubro, com a chegada do Papai Noel.
articles.body:
Evento começa no dia 30 de outubro — Foto: Divulgação/FLMA

A programação de Natal 2026 de Campos do Jordão, no interior de São Paulo, começa no dia 30 de outubro com a chegada do Papai Noel e uma carreata que marcará o acendimento das luzes da cidade.

Segundo a Fundação Lia Maria Aguiar, serão mais de 16 quilômetros de luzes, cerca de 300 esculturas natalinas e uma árvore de Natal de 20 metros de altura, na Praça do Capivari.

O evento terá atrações até 20 de dezembro. O investimento na decoração foi de R$ 5 milhões. A decoração será instalada no Portal da cidade, na Praça Abernéssia e na Praça do Capivari, onde ficará a Casa do Papai Noel.

Neste ano, a programação terá como tema a “Fábrica de Biscoitos” e contará com novas atrações, mudanças nos locais dos espetáculos e ampliação da decoração natalina.

Durante o período, Campos do Jordão receberá dezenas de apresentações artísticas e concertos sinfônicos, com participação de alunos dos Núcleos de Dança, Música e Teatro da Fundação Lia Maria Aguiar.

Campos do Jordão terá árvore natalina de 20 metros e 16 quilômetros de luzes — Foto: Divulgação/FLMA

Uma das mudanças para 2026 será o local dos espetáculos dos Núcleos de Música, Dança e Teatro. As apresentações, que anteriormente eram realizadas em outros espaços, passarão a acontecer no Campos Hall, espaço de eventos localizado a cerca de 300 metros do centro do bairro Capivari.

O local tem capacidade para 2,5 mil pessoas e conta com estrutura de banheiros, acessibilidade e conforto térmico.

Os espetáculos serão realizados às sextas-feiras, sábados e domingos, entre 31 de outubro e 20 de dezembro.

A programação artística começa em 31 de outubro com o concerto “Uma Noite de Luz”, apresentado pela Orquestra e pelo Coro Artístico.

O espetáculo será apresentado durante dois finais de semana, até 8 de novembro, com a participação de cerca de cem alunos do Núcleo de Música.

A partir de 13 de novembro, será apresentado o espetáculo “O Melhor Presente”, que reúne a Companhia de Teatro e os Núcleos de Dança e Música.

A produção terá figurinos, objetos cênicos e recursos de LED integrados ao cenário. A história aborda relações familiares e temas como presença, afeto e vínculos entre as pessoas.

articles.title: The Town 2027 anuncia Slipknot e Marilyn Manson como atrações | G1
articles.standfirst: Bandas se apresentarão no palco Skyline no dia 4 de setembro; festival volta a Interlagos, em São Paulo.
articles.summary: O festival The Town 2027 confirmou Slipknot e Marilyn Manson no palco Skyline para o dia 4 de setembro, marcando o retorno do evento ao Autódromo de Interlagos.
articles.body:
Slipknot e Marilyn Manson estarão no The Town 2027 — Foto: Flávio Moraes/G1 e AP

O The Town 2027 anunciou as duas primeiras atrações do festival: Slipknot e Marilyn Manson. Os dois se apresentarão no palco principal do evento, o Skyline, no dia 4 de setembro.

A apresentação do Slipknot vai integrar uma turnê global da banda, também anunciada nesta segunda-feira (28), e será a única realizada em um festival.

Chegando à sua terceira edição, o The Town acontecerá nos dias 4, 5, 6, 11 e 12 de setembro de 2027 no Autódromo de Interlagos, em São Paulo.

Ainda não há informações sobre venda de ingressos.

articles.title: ‘Avengers: Endgame’ retakes box office crown; Robert Pattinson drives sales for ‘Primetime’
articles.summary: Seven years after becoming the second-highest grossing film ever, “Avengers: Endgame” returned to the No. 1 spot at the box office in a victory lap for Marvel and an appetizer for the upcoming blockbuster “Avengers: Doomsday.”
articles.body: NEW YORK — Seven years after becoming the second-highest grossing film ever, “Avengers: Endgame” returned to the No. 1 spot at the box office in a victory lap for Marvel and an appetizer for the upcoming blockbuster “Avengers: Doomsday.” The rerelease grossed $26 million over the weekend and another $60 million overseas, according to studio estimates Sunday. The film, which grossed $2.8 billion in 2019, was put back into theaters with several new end-credits scenes and an introductory thank you to fans from Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans. Among rereleases, only the 1997 release of “Star Wars: A New Hope” ($35.9 million) and the 2011 repeat of “The Lion King” ($30.2 million) have opened higher than “Endgame” in domestic cinemas. Hollywood has increasingly turned to rereleases in recent years to take advantage of holes in the release schedule. But The Walt Disney Co. rerun, billed as “Endgame: Encore,” came out on top on an especially crowded weekend in theaters. Three well-reviewed new releases — A24’s “Primetime,” with Robert Pattinson; Paramount Pictures’ “Heart of the Beast,” with Brad Pitt; and Universal Pictures’ “Forgotten Island” — all landed in theaters. Second place, though, went to Zach Cregger’s reboot of “Resident Evil.” The Sony Pictures release followed up its above-expectations debut with $23.3 million in its second weekend. In two weeks, the video-game adaptation has grossed $103.5 million in U.S. and Canadian theaters. In a close race for third place, “Heart of the Beast” came out just ahead of “Primetime” with an estimated $20 million from 3,435 theaters. Directed by David Ayer, the film stars Pitt as a retired veteran who must trek through the Alaskan wilderness with his combat dog after a plane crash. It added $30.1 million in international theaters. Pattinson drives ‘Primetime’ sales But the opening for “Primetime” was more impressive. “Heart of the Beast” cost $82 million to produce, making its path to profitability challenging. “Primetime,” starring Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, was made with a modest budget of $15 million and it opened in 500 fewer theaters. Yet “Primetime,” buoyed by strong reviews and buzz out of the Venice Film Festival, debuted with $19.2 million. For Pattinson, who also starred this year in A24’s “The Drama” and Universal’s “The Odyssey,” the strong performance showed the actor’s drawing power with Gen Z audiences. Some 69% of ticket buyers for “Primetime” were under the age of 30. Gen Z has emerged as the most regular moviegoing demographic, fueling hits this year like “Obsession” and “Backrooms.” “Primetime” is directed by 30-year-old documentarian Lance Oppenheim, who co-directed the much-anticipated Elizabeth Holmes documentary, “You Can See Everything,” due out next month. “Forgotten Island,” from DreamWorks Animation, had a hard time standing out. The film, which cost $80 million to make, opened in fifth place with a disappointing $12.8 million domestically. In 31 overseas markets, “Forgotten Island” also didn’t make much of a dent, grossing $7.8 million internationally. Universal will hope family audiences catch up to the movie that landed the weekend’s best CinemaScore (an “A”) and the best reviews (94% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes). “Forgotten Island,” directed by Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado, is about two friends who get stranded in a mystical world. The confluence of releases added up to a historically good September weekend in theaters. According to Rentrak, ticket sales were up 58.5% from the same weekend last year. The domestic box office has massed $7.8 billion thus far, putting it 19% ahead of last year. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Avengers: Endgame: Encore,” $26 million. 2. “Resident Evil,” $23.3 million. 3. “Heart of the Beast,” $20 million. 4. “Primetime,” $19.2 million. 5. “Forgotten Island,” $12.8 million. 6. “Practical Magic 2,” $5.7 million. 7. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” $4.1 million. 8. “The Odyssey,” $3.7 million. 9. “Coyote vs. Acme,” $1.9 million. 10. “Daniel and the Fiery Furnace,” $1.5 million.

articles.title: Taylor Swift premieres music video for 'Patient Zero' at the VMAs
articles.summary: Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell star in this track off the encore edition of Swift's 12th album, "The Life of a Showgirl."
articles.body:
Taylor Swift's new video for "Patient Zero" has officially arrived, and it may be her darkest yet.

Swift premiered the new video at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday after dropping a teaser for the project days earlier on social media. The song is one of the four tracks off the encore edition of Swift's 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl , which she released on Sept. 25.

The moody, psychological thriller-inspired "Patient Zero" video stars Swift alongside Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell. In the video, Johnson plays the wife of a wealthy businessman (Farrell) who begins to suspect that her perfect husband may be manipulating and gaslighting her. Swift portrays his previous wife, an heiress who, at the end of the video, is revealed to have been killed by Farrell's character. The ghost of Swift's character attempts to warn Johnson's to "run" before it's too late.

Also appearing in the video briefly is Cara Delevingne, a longtime pal of Swift's, who plays the "other woman" whom Johnson's character suspects of flirting with her husband.

In an Instagram post , Swift said the video was influenced by "the cinematic and literary genres I love so much," including gothic ghost stories and psychological thrillers.

This is the first time Swift and Johnson have worked together, but the two are friends. They were spotted out to dinner together in New York City in 2025, and this April, Swift penned an essay praising Johnson when the Materialists star made Time's 2026 list of 100 most influential people.

"As her friend, I can vouch for her realness, but add that she's also one of the most empathetic people I've ever known," Swift wrote at the time.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Sept. 24, Johnson called filming the music video "the best."

"It's so much fun to work with your friends," she said. "Like I love hanging out with her, so hanging out and making stuff is really fun."

In an interview with the Fan Girl Nation alongside her Verity costar Josh Hartnett, Johnson again shared that the experience of making "Patient Zero" was "so fun."

"Taylor and I have been friends for a really long time, and we're very close, and we decided to work together," she said. "And it's great. Like normally, I would say don't work your work with your friends, but we work really well together."

This video shares thematic similarities to Johnson's upcoming film Verity , a psychological thriller based on Colleen Hoover's 2018 novel of the same name. In the film, out Oct. 2, Johnson plays a writer named Lowen tasked with taking over a mystery series from Anne Hathaway's titular character . articles.title: King Charles, Prince William 'furious' as Princess Diana's brother unleashes explosive claims: experts
articles.summary: Charles Spencer's "Swan Song" reopens royal family wounds with claims about Princess Diana's funeral that have rattled Buckingham Palace insiders.
articles.body: King Charles III and Prince William are said to be furious at Charles Spencer's new book, which makes damning allegations about the monarch and reopens decades-old wounds within the royal family. The claim was made by several royal experts who spoke to Fox News Digital after "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" was published on Tuesday. In it, Princess Diana's brother says he argued with then-Prince Charles over palace plans to have William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, walk behind their mother's coffin during her 1997 funeral procession. Most notably, Spencer alleged that after Diana died at age 36 in a car crash, Charles "sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner." He wrote that Charles "went ballistic" during an argument they had over William and Harry. Spencer said Charles then hissed, "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough." KING CHARLES RESPONDS TO CHARLES SPENCER'S CLAIMS ABOUT PRINCESS DIANA IN A RARE STATEMENT "What I am hearing concerning the reaction around both households is frustration and anger, but for slightly different reasons," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "For the king, I think there is genuine anger at what amounts to an attack on his character almost 30 years after Diana's death," she explained. "But Charles has also lived with being cast as the villain in the Diana story for decades. Unfortunately, being portrayed as the bad guy in somebody else's version of this story is not new territory for him. For Prince William, there is an additional sense of betrayal. This is his uncle, who famously stood at Diana's funeral and promised that her 'blood family' would protect William and Harry." After excerpts from the book were published last week, Buckingham Palace issued a rare, strongly worded statement. "His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said. A spokesperson for Buckingham Palace told Fox News Digital it had no comment. A spokesperson for Kensington Palace previously told Fox News Digital the palace does not comment on books. Spencer has stood by his account, insisting to the BBC that he is telling the truth. He asked, "Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" Some critics have questioned why Spencer felt the need to revisit the pain and trauma nearly 30 years later, The Associated Press reported. Author Christopher Andersen told Fox News Digital he was surprised by Spencer's allegations. "Just weeks after Diana was killed, I interviewed hundreds of sources in London and Paris for my book 'The Day Diana Died,'" he said. "They all remembered that Charles was absolutely devastated. 'Crushed' was a word I heard repeatedly when he first learned the news of Diana's death. After years of famously battling as a married couple, they had finally found a kind of peace with each other following their 1996 divorce. They actually became friends." "When Charles got the call at Balmoral that Diana had been killed, a staffer told me that the king let out a howl that sounded like a wounded animal, then burst into tears. Others described Charles at the time as being racked with sobs, his face streaked with tears." "I also interviewed the nurses at the Paris hospital who witnessed the moment Charles saw Diana's body for the first time," Andersen continued. "He fell back, one of them told me, as if he had been struck by an unseen hand. They thought he was going to pass out. He then began to weep openly. She refused to fly the flag at half-staff over Buckingham Palace in Diana's honor. She did not even want to come back from her summer vacation at Balmoral. It fell on Charles' shoulders to force his mother to show Diana the respect the British people felt she deserved." Still, Andersen said he would not be surprised if the king had shouted hurtful words at Spencer in anger. "Charles has a long history of lashing out, making rash and sometimes cruel, offhand statements," Andersen said. "The king always resented being overshadowed by Diana during her lifetime, and now he was being totally eclipsed by her in death. There was lingering resentment there. It's also clear the king knew that the public would blame him and Camilla for making Diana so desperately unhappy during her lifetime and, to some extent, for the extent, for the events leading up to her death." Andersen noted that the late queen "was in no mood" to see her eldest son remarry anytime soon. People experienced those events from very different perspectives, and she recognizes that emotions surrounding Diana are still exceptionally powerful." British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that William isn't close to his uncle and that sources have told her he is "absolutely furious." "His public silence regarding this matter is admirable," she said. "The pain Spencer is causing William has backfired as he’s being accused of monetizing his sister’s memory." articles.title: In 1992, Arnold Schwarzenegger wanted to give children a safe place after school; 34 years later, his initiative serves over 140,000 students
articles.summary: Long before Arnold Schwarzenegger became California’s governor, he was already working on an issue involving children and the hours they spent outside
articles.body: Long before Arnold Schwarzenegger became California’s governor, he was already working on an issue involving children and the hours they spent outside school. In 1992, Schwarzenegger and Danny Hernandez founded the Inner-City Games Foundation, an initiative that brought sports and fitness activities to young people in under-resourced communities.More than three decades later, that initiative has evolved into After-School All-Stars (ASAS), a national nonprofit providing free after-school and summer programmes. According to its latest figures, the organisation now reaches 140,833 students annually through 754 sites across 77 US cities.The organisation’s beginnings were rooted in the idea that children’s lives did not stop when the school bell rang. Its early programmes used sports and physical activities to provide young people with organised experiences during after-school hours.The Los Angeles chapter was established in 1992, and the organisation received its official 501(c)(3) nonprofit designation the following year. Over the next few years, chapters were established in cities including Atlanta, Las Vegas, Orlando, New York City and San Diego.From sports programmes to broader education supportThe initiative gradually became more ambitious. In 2003, the Inner-City Games expanded its mission to comprehensive, school-based programming and adopted the name After-School All-Stars.Its work now extends well beyond athletics. ASAS offers programmes covering academic support, STEM, visual and performing arts, health and wellness, and career exploration. Students can take part in activities ranging from homework assistance and coding to music, sports, cooking and career-focused experiences.The organisation also introduced programmes aimed at helping teenagers prepare for life beyond school. CampUS, launched in 2010, focused on high school and college success, while STEM CampUs followed in 2013 with activities connected to fields including engineering, graphic design and applied sciences. The same year, ASAS launched its national Youth Advisory Board, giving participating students a role in shaping programmes and community-service initiatives. The organisation reported serving 95,502 students in 2012. By 2021, its summer programming had expanded to 212 sites and reached nearly 11,000 students.In 2002, while campaigning in California, he backed Proposition 49, the After School Education and Safety Act. California voters approved the measure, which provided $550 million for after-school programmes for students in kindergarten through ninth grade, according to the ASAS timeline and the USC Schwarzenegger Institute.The USC Schwarzenegger Institute has also reported that Schwarzenegger spent $2.3 million of his own money supporting the campaign for the measure. His advocacy continued after his time in California politics. At the 2017 National Afterschool Summit, Schwarzenegger urged leaders to oppose proposed federal cuts to after-school funding and described the period between 3 p.m. and 6 p.m. as a particularly important period for young people.“This is not a party issue, this is a people’s issue,” Schwarzenegger said at the summit. During the event, he also referred to concerns raised by law enforcement about young people being exposed to drugs, alcohol, gangs and violence during unsupervised after-school hours.The organisation’s reach continues to expandASAS has continued adding academic, career, health and enrichment opportunities to its programmes. Its current work is spread across schools and other community locations, including recreation centres and housing authorities.The organisation’s FY24 annual report highlighted programmes operating at 740 sites, with nearly 150,000 students participating during that year. Its financial timeline also states that annual revenue crossed $100 million in 2024, rising from $91.5 million in 2023 to $104.7 million, with the organisation reporting that 89% of revenue went directly to programmes.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. Stop using my name to serve your agenda. May God protect every decent man from such cunning women."Govinda and Komal Rani Swarnkar are working together on his upcoming comeback film titled 'Roopa'. articles.title: Rosie O’Donnell rips Ed Sheeran for ‘siding with billionaire elite,’ accuses him of ‘supporting genocide’
articles.summary: Rosie O'Donnell accused Ed Sheeran of siding with Robert Kraft and of "supporting genocide" after Macklemore was dropped from the "Loop Tour."
articles.body: Rosie O'Donnell blasted New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and singer Ed Sheeran on Friday during an appearance on Ireland's "The Late Late Show," accusing Sheeran of making a "very bad mistake" after Macklemore was removed from his U.S. tour following the rapper's pro-Palestinian performances. O’Donnell made the accusation after host Patrick Kielty asked about the controversy surrounding Kraft, Sheeran and Macklemore. "I think Ed Sheeran made a very bad mistake and that he will come to understand the ramifications of siding with a billionaire elite, in supporting genocide rather than the people who are saying, 'This is wrong. We will not stand for it. We are human beings and each human life matters and that's what's the most important thing,'" O’Donnell said. LIBERAL LAWMAKERS, ACTIVISTS RALLY BEHIND MACKLEMORE AFTER SHEERAN TOUR REMOVAL OVER 'FREE PALESTINE' STANCE "Hollywood in Toto" host Christian Toto said celebrities face pressure within the entertainment industry to adopt a particular position on the Israel-Palestinian conflict and compared the dynamic to the entertainment industry’s response to Black Lives Matter. "There is only one acceptable answer for celebrities when it comes to the ongoing Israel/Palestinian conflict. Say 'Free Palestine' and nothing else," Toto told Fox News Digital in comments Sunday. "It's the new BLM, a contentious issue where celebrities know they'll gain approval within their circle by repeating that mantra. They also understand they won't be pressured to defend their point of view by the vast majority of entertainment reporters. It's a safe space for them. Journalists now know they can pepper stars with similar questions and get a similar response (and lots of clicks for their interviews)." "Most artists know better than to alienate audiences with their political views," he continued. "The Springsteens, Morellos and Macklemores remain the exception. Concert ticket prices are too high for most bands to get on their soapbox and risk dooming repeat business. Actors don't make the connection between their divisive words and audience reaction. They simply want to appease their fellow actors and make nice with potential directors and casting directors. So they read from the approved script." ED SHEERAN FACES GROWING BACKLASH AS RADIO STATION BANS SONGS, PROTEST GROUPS RESPOND TO MACKLEMORE'S REMOVAL O'Donnell directly targeted Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium and founded the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, after Kielty referenced Kraft's role in opposing Macklemore's appearance at the venue. "Well, he's part of the billionaire elite," she said. "Those are the most corrupt people in the United States right now. And they have sort of performed a coup on the American government. And it's very tragic." Nick Fondacaro, associate editor for NewsBusters, reacted to O'Donnell's comments, saying, "Are we surprised that an unabashed 9/11-truther took an irrational and unhinged position?" "It’s irresponsible and incendiary to claim a coup has taken place in America, especially when political violence is on the rise. Given that people like Charlie Kirk and Brian Thompson have been killed by leftists for their political causes, Rosie’s prediction that Sheeran will come to learn a lesson sounded like a warning or threat," he continued. "It’s hypocritical that a multimillionaire like Rosie things that Robert Kraft didn’t have the same rights as she and Macklemore. The stadium is his property, and he can decide who to allow in or not, just like they can bar Kraft from their multimillion-dollar mansions." Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran's "Loop Tour" after repeatedly saying "Free Palestine" and performing "Hind's Hall" during shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The rapper alleged Kraft told Sheeran he would not be permitted to perform at Gillette Stadium and rallied other venue owners against his continued participation. Tour promoter Messina Touring Group said venues had informed them they would not allow concerts to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup. ROBERT KRAFT, GILLETTE STADIUM BOOT MACKLEMORE FROM ED SHEERAN TOUR OVER ‘FREE PALESTINE’ RANT Kraft defended his position by citing what he described as Macklemore's "broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery," while stressing that his decision was not intended to dismiss Palestinian suffering. Kraft said support for Palestinians and opposition to Hamas and antisemitism were compatible positions. "Standing with the Palestinian people and standing against Hamas, antisemitism and hate should not be mutually exclusive," Kraft said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Sheeran has also publicly rejected the implication that he supports the suffering of Palestinians. During his first concert after the controversy, Fox News Digital reported from Philadelphia that Sheeran condemned Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack while also criticizing the scale of civilian suffering in Gaza. "What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate," Sheeran said. Sheeran also pledged $2 million toward humanitarian relief and asked Kraft to match the contribution. Kraft agreed, saying he had spent decades supporting programs bringing Palestinians and Israelis together. Macklemore separately pledged the $1 million he said he earned from the tour to Palestinian aid organizations. articles.title: Matthew Stafford makes surprise cameo in Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ music video
articles.summary: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford made a surprise appearance in Taylor Swift's music video for 'Patient Zero', premiered at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards. Find out how this crossover event links the NFL to Swift's music world.
articles.body: Matthew Stafford had a very different kind of spotlight waiting for him before his Sunday Night Football game. The Los Angeles Rams quarterback made a surprise appearance in Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ music video, which premiered during the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards on Sunday, September 27, 2026. The cameo caught fans off guard, especially because Stafford’s appearance was not revealed in the first teaser for the video.Taylor Swift’s new music video stars Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell, with the singer herself also appearing throughout the dark, cinematic story. Stafford and his wife, Kelly Stafford, also make brief appearances in the video.Matthew Stafford appears in Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ music videoMatthew Stafford pops up several times in the video. In one scene, he is seen shaking hands with Colin Farrell’s character, while another shot shows him standing alongside the actor on a stage. The Rams quarterback also appears in the background dancing with his wife, Kelly Stafford. The surprise cameo was first reported after the video premiered at the 2026 MTV VMAs. USA TODAY noted that fans were initially expecting to see mainly Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell after Swift’s first teaser was released.Why was Matthew Stafford in Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ video?The cameo also makes sense when you look at Matthew Stafford’s connection to Swift and her wider circle. Matthew and Kelly Stafford were among the celebrities who attended Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding earlier this summer. The Rams quarterback is also one of the biggest names in Los Angeles sports, making his appearance a fun crossover between the NFL and Swift’s music world.Stafford’s cameo also contained a little Easter egg of its own. Fans connected his appearance to the word “Aries” from Swift’s earlier ‘Law & Order’-themed sketch, with Aries being the zodiac sign associated with the ram a nod to the Los Angeles Rams. Swifties quickly picked up on the clue after the music video premiered.Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ video stars Dakota Johnson and Colin FarrellThe main story of ‘Patient Zero’ centres on Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell. Johnson plays a woman who becomes involved with Farrell’s character, while Swift appears as his former wife. The video has a dark, almost gothic feel, mixing elements of a psychological thriller, ghost story and true crime.The story eventually reveals a much darker twist involving Farrell’s character and Swift’s death. Swift has said the video allowed her to explore several genres she enjoys. In an Instagram post after the premiere, she explained that the house featured in the video was also meant to represent “the coldness of a relationship that’s faded and atrophied.”Cara Delevingne also makes a brief appearance in the music video‘Patient Zero’ premiered at the 2026 MTV VMAs. Taylor Swift premiered ‘Patient Zero’ at the MTV Video Music Awards on September 27, 2026, shortly after accepting the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors. The video was part of a particularly big night for Swift, who also received multiple nominations at the 2026 ceremony. The song itself was released on September 25, 2026, as part of ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’, which features four additional tracks: ‘Patient Zero’, ‘Cleveland!’, ‘Pink Clouding’ and ‘Babylon’. Matthew Stafford makes NFL history after Taylor Swift cameo.Matthew Stafford’s Taylor Swift cameo was only one part of a very busy Sunday for the quarterback. Just hours after appearing in the ‘Patient Zero’ music video, Stafford took the field with the Los Angeles Rams against the Denver Broncos on Sunday Night Football. During the game, he became the first quarterback in NFL history to throw for more than 20,000 passing yards with two different teams. Stafford had previously crossed the 20,000-yard mark during his time with the Detroit Lions in 2014. He reached the milestone with the Rams during the Broncos game after completing a 15-yard pass to wide receiver Konata Mumpfield in the second quarter.The milestone came despite a difficult night for Stafford and the Rams. He finished with 390 passing yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions as Los Angeles eventually lost 30-26 to Denver.Within the space of a few hours, Stafford went from appearing alongside Taylor Swift and Colin Farrell in a major new music video to making NFL history on Sunday Night Football.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Elizabeth Holmes Posts Cryptic Message From Prison Ahead of ‘You Can See Everything’ Release: ‘I Was Silenced for a Long Time’
articles.summary: Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, who’s been serving an 11-year prison sentence for fraud, posted a mysterious message on X ahead of moving to a halfway hou...
articles.body:
Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, who's been serving an 11-year prison sentence for fraud, posted a mysterious message on X ahead of moving to a halfway house and the release of a new documentary about her, "You Can See Everything," from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

Holmes has still been active on X since her 2022 sentencing thanks to her social media team; her bio says "mostly my words, posted by others." Now, it seems the businesswoman, fraudster and documentary subject will be posting her some of her messages herself.

"I was silenced for a long time. And then imprisoned. I am fighting to prove my innocence and come home to my babies and the love of my life. I have now been imprisoned for 1,216 endless days and nights. During that time, as we fight for freedom, my loved ones have helped manage my account. Billy is one of the people carrying that responsibility for me. He fights fiercely for me and our family. I love him beyond space and time. Starting now, all posts in my own words will be marked -EAH. Posts without that signature are from the team managing this account."

Holmes, who signed the post with her initials "-EAH," shared a photo of herself and her partner Billy Evans, with whom she has two children. In "You Can See Everything," she and Evans invited Fielder and Oppenheim into their home ahead of Holmes' prison sentence to document their lives. The A24 film releases on Oct. 16, but it's already drawn huge buzz after its surprise debut at this month's Telluride Film Festival. It will screen at the New York Film Festival this week.

Holmes' post also comes on the heels of her announced move to a halfway house next summer. Last week, a judge approved Holmes' transfer too the Austin Transitional Center, a halfway house in Del Valle, Texas, on August 23, 2027. She's been staying at the Federal Prison Camp, Bryan, a minimum-security facility in Bryan, Texas, and is scheduled to be released on Feb. 22, 2030, roughly four years early due to good behavior.

"I am profoundly grateful for the support we receive as we fight to expose the truth and challenge deeply entrenched perceptions," Holmes wrote. "Opening letters from my supporters at the end of unforgiving days constantly ignites the fire in my heart. 'The truth will set you free.' John 8:32."

articles.title: In 2000, Michael J. Fox started a foundation after his Parkinson’s diagnosis; 26 years later, it has funded more than $3 billion in research
articles.summary: Actor Michael J. Fox turned a life-changing diagnosis into a long-term mission to accelerate Parkinson’s research. In 2000, he established The Michael J.
articles.body: Actor Michael J. Fox turned a life-changing diagnosis into a long-term mission to accelerate Parkinson’s research. In 2000, he established The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, nearly a decade after he was diagnosed with the disease.Fox was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 1991 at the age of 29. He initially kept the diagnosis private and publicly revealed that he was living with Parkinson’s in 1998. Two years later, he founded the organisation with the aim of accelerating scientific progress towards better treatments and, ultimately, a cure.More than two and a half decades later, the foundation has grown into the world’s largest nonprofit funder of Parkinson’s research. According to the organisation, it has funded more than $3 billion in research globally since its inception in 2000.The foundation says its work focuses on accelerating the development of treatments by funding research, bringing together scientists, industry and patients, and supporting initiatives that can move discoveries from laboratories towards clinical applications.One of its major research initiatives is the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), a global study designed to better understand the biology of Parkinson’s and identify markers that could help researchers develop and test treatments. The foundation says the initiative has contributed to scientific advances in understanding the disease.The organisation has also pointed to progress in Parkinson’s treatment over the years. In a September 2026 update, it said its research efforts had contributed to a pipeline that includes 175 therapies in clinical testing and noted that 23 new drugs had been approved over the past decade. These figures describe developments across the broader Parkinson’s research ecosystem and are not claims that all of the drugs were developed solely by the foundation.Fox’s advocacy has extended beyond funding research. In 1999, before establishing the foundation, he testified before the US Congress in support of greater federal investment in Parkinson’s research. The foundation later supported advocacy efforts around the National Plan to End Parkinson’s Act, which became law in July 2024.In September 2026, Fox was also named the recipient of the Lasker~Bloomberg Public Service Award for his contributions to advancing Parkinson’s research and raising awareness about the disease. The award recognised his work in advocacy, philanthropy and research mobilisation.From a diagnosis he received at just 29 to a foundation that has now directed more than $3 billion towards Parkinson’s research, Fox’s journey has become closely associated with efforts to accelerate scientific progress against the disease.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more.
